entry: Physics of the cause–effect relation. Causality requires that the cause of an event lie in the past light cone of its result and be ultimately reducible to [[Fundamental interaction|fundamental interactions]]; a cause cannot have an effect outside its future light cone. The weak causality principle operates at the microscopic level and need not lead to information transfer, whereas the strong principle forbids information transfer faster than the [[Speed of light|speed of light]]. In [[Special relativity]], the cause must precede its effect for all inertial observers, since a faster-than-light signal would travel backward in time for some of them. [[General relativity]] extends the rule to curved spacetime. In quantum field theory, microcausality requires that measurements at spacelike-separated points cannot affect each other. [[Bell's theorem]] shows that local causality, tested in experiments on [[Quantum entanglement|quantum entanglement]], produces non-classical correlations predicted by [[Quantum mechanics]].

Mounted soldiers or warriors. Cavalry was historically divided into light and heavy cavalry, distinguished by combat role, mount size and the armor worn by rider and horse. Riding gave cavalry greater height, speed and inertial mass than an opponent on foot, advantages valued in the ancient and medieval eras. Heavy cavalry, such as Byzantine cataphracts and European [[Knight|knights]], served as shock troops, while light cavalry, including horse archers, hussars and Cossack units, handled scouting, raiding and skirmishing. The [[Huns]] of [[Attila]] and later Mongol armies were mostly cavalry. European cavalry discarded most of its [[Armour|armor]] in the 17th century, which was ineffective against muskets and cannon. Many units became [[Infantry|motorized infantry]] or [[Tank|tank]] troops between the world wars. Modern horse-mounted cavalry serves mainly in ceremonial roles, and the term now usually refers to reconnaissance units or main battle tank units.

Natural void under a planetary surface. Caves form mainly by the weathering of rock and can extend deep underground; they have also been observed on other rocky worlds, such as Mars. Exogene caves are short openings such as rock shelters, while endogene caves extend farther underground than they are wide. The scientific study of caves is speleology. Most caves are solutional, or karst, caves formed when acidic [[Groundwater|groundwater]] dissolves soluble rock, most often [[Limestone|limestone]], along bedding planes and faults. Dissolution produces [[Karst|karst]] landscapes with [[Sinkhole|sinkholes]] and underground drainage, and limestone caves often contain [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]] formations such as stalactites and stalagmites. [[Lava|Lava]] tubes form when the surface of a flow cools and the molten interior drains away. Lechuguilla Cave in [[New Mexico]] is believed to have formed when hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) gas from below mixed with groundwater to form sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄).

Parietal art, usually prehistoric, on the walls and ceilings of caverns. Parietal art also includes [[Engraving|engravings]], or petroglyphs, and some paintings may have been made by species other than *Homo sapiens*. Nearly 350 [[Cave|caves]] in France and Spain contain prehistoric art. Radiocarbon dating can mislead when samples are contaminated, so later work sampled the pigment itself, torch marks or [[Carbonate|carbonate]] deposits that formed over the art. The oldest claimed cave painting is a stencil or handprint on Muna Island, dated at least 67,800 years old. The oldest figurative cave painting, showing human figures hunting pigs in the Maros-Pangkep karst of South [[Sulawesi]], [[Indonesia]], is dated to more than 43,900 years old. In [[South Africa|South Africa]], hand-drawn lines on a rock excavated from a site are dated to 73,000 years. Paintings at Chauvet Cave in France were modified repeatedly, and radiocarbon dates show two periods of creation, 35,000 and 30,000 years ago.

High-power [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tube]] for generating microwaves. Electrons moving past a series of cavity resonators in a metal block interact with a magnetic field to produce microwaves, at a frequency set by the cavities' dimensions. Unlike an [[Amplifier|amplifier]] tube, it serves only as an oscillator. A cavity magnetron introduced by John Randall and Harry Boot at the University of Birmingham in 1940 was an improvement; engineers at [[General Electric|GEC]] raised its output to well over a kilowatt within weeks and to 25 kW within months. Its high-power pulses reduced practical [[Radar|radar]] systems by orders of magnitude, and radars could be installed in fighter aircraft. By the end of [[World War II]], practically every [[Allies of World War II|Allied]] radar was based on the magnetron. It fell from favor in the 1960s as high-power klystrons emerged, but over one billion magnetrons are now in use, mostly in [[Microwave oven|microwave ovens]].

Hot chili pepper variety used as a spice. Cayenne peppers are tapering, mostly red, 10 to 25 cm long, and generally rated at 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville units. They are a type of *Capsicum annuum*, the species that also includes [[Bell pepper|bell peppers]] and [[Jalapeño|jalapeños]]. The dried, ground fruits make the powdered spice, which may be a blend that does not contain cayenne. The fruits are rich in provitamin A, [[Carotenoid|carotenoids]] and [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]], and the [[Capsaicin|capsaicin]] they contain gives the pepper its heat.

Self-governing [[British Overseas Territories|British Overseas Territory]] in the western Caribbean. The territory comprises Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman, with the capital, George Town, on Grand Cayman. The name derives from the word for crocodile, [[Caiman|caiman]], in the language of the Arawak-Taíno people. [[Christopher Columbus]] is believed to have been the first European to sight the islands, on May 10, 1503. England took formal control in 1670, and a permanent English-speaking population dates from the 1730s. [[Slavery|Slavery]] was abolished in 1833. From 1863 the islands were a dependency of the Crown Colony of [[Jamaica]], becoming a separate Crown colony in 1962. The territory charges no tax on income, and it is a major tax haven; critics allege that it facilitates tax evasion.

Highly urbanized city (pop., 2024: 965,332) in the Central Visayas region of the Philippines. It is the capital of Cebu province but is administratively independent of the provincial government, and it serves as the regional center of Central Visayas. Its [[Metropolitan area|metropolitan area]] influences commerce, education and healthcare across Central and Eastern [[Visayas|Visayas]] and partly over [[Mindanao|Mindanao]]. It is the Philippines' main domestic shipping port and the core city of Metro Cebu, the second largest metropolitan area in the Philippines. The modern name Cebu is a Spanish pronunciation of the native name Sugbo. [[Ferdinand Magellan]] arrived on April 7, 1521. Rapid economic growth since the 1990s, a phenomenon known as Ceboom, has earned the city the popular name Queen City of the South.

Austronesian language of the Philippines. Cebuano is spoken natively by the Visayan people and used as a second language by other ethnic groups across Cebu, Bohol, Negros and much of [[Mindanao|Mindanao]]. It is the [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] of Central Visayas and most of Mindanao. Although Tagalog has more native speakers today, Cebuano had the largest native-speaking population from the 1950s until about the 1980s, and it is by far the most widely spoken of the Bisayan languages. Some speakers in parts of Leyte and Mindanao object to the name Cebuano and prefer Bisayâ or Binisayâ, while others argue that the name should be kept. The language is not widely spoken in [[Luzon|Luzon]], although communities exist in [[Metro Manila]].

American filmmaker and [[Actor|actor]]. He is acknowledged as a founding figure of American cinema and one of the most commercially successful producer-directors in film history, known for epic-scale films and cinematic showmanship. He created 70 features, beginning with *The Squaw Man* (1914), the first full-length feature shot in Hollywood. DeMille founded Famous Players-Lasky, which was later reverse merged into [[Paramount Pictures]]. His biblical epic *The Ten Commandments* (1923) held the Paramount revenue record for 25 years. *The King of Kings* (1927) reached more than 800 million viewers, and *Samson and Delilah* (1949) was the highest-grossing film of 1950. *The Greatest Show on Earth* (1952) won the Academy Award for Best Picture, and his 1956 remake of *The Ten Commandments* became his best-known film.

British mining magnate and politician in southern Africa. Rhodes entered the diamond trade at Kimberley in 1871 and bought out diamond mines until he gained a near-complete monopoly of the world diamond market. He founded De Beers in 1888. He served as prime minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896. His British South Africa Company founded the territory of [[Rhodesia|Rhodesia]], named after him in 1895, which is now [[Zimbabwe]] and [[Zambia]]. As prime minister he passed the Glen Grey Act, which took land from Black Africans, and tripled the wealth requirement for voting. Critics cite these measures, which effectively barred Black people from elections, and his promotion of claims that [[Great Zimbabwe|Great Zimbabwe]] was built by Europeans. He resigned in 1896 after the Jameson Raid, an unauthorized attack on the South African Republic. His will endowed the Rhodes Scholarship at the [[University of Oxford|University of Oxford]].

Genus of coniferous trees known as cedars. The genus belongs to the pine family, Pinaceae, and contains between one and four species, depending on taxonomic opinion. The trees are native to the mountains of the western [[Himalayas|Himalayas]] and the Mediterranean region, including the [[Atlas Mountains|Atlas Mountains]]. They grow to 30–40 m (100–130 ft), with cylindrical trunks and needle-like leaves in tufts of 15–45. The cones are erect and disintegrate at maturity to release winged seeds, and both pollen and seeds are wind-dispersed. Cedar wood and cedarwood oil repel moths. The English name derives from Latin *cedrus*, from Greek *kédros*, a word that may first have applied to [[Juniper|juniper]]. Cedars are often grown as bonsai.

Oral first-generation cephalosporin [[Antibiotic|antibiotic]]. Cefalexin, also spelled cephalexin, kills gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria by disrupting the growth of the bacterial [[Cell wall|cell wall]]. It treats infections of the middle ear, bone and joint, skin and urinary tract, and may be used for some [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] and strep throat. It is not effective against methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* or viral infections such as the [[Common cold|common cold]]. It can be used in people with mild or moderate [[Penicillin|penicillin]] allergies. Developed in 1967 and first marketed in 1969 as Keflex, it is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines.

Overhead interior surface concealing the underside of the [[Roof|roof]] structure or the floor above. A ceiling can also be the upper limit of a [[Tunnel|tunnel]]. The most common type is the dropped ceiling, suspended from structural elements above and usually finished with drywall, leaving space above for pipework, ducts and insulation. A suspended ceiling uses aluminum struts and removable panels, which make repairs behind it easier. Other types include the cathedral, coffered, concave and stretched ceiling. Dropped ceilings can contribute to a building's fire-resistance rating. Many ceilings have been decorated with fresco painting and [[Mosaic|mosaic]] tiles, and perhaps the most famous is the [[Sistine Chapel]] ceiling by [[Michelangelo]].

Condition of fame and broad public recognition. Celebrity status can come from great wealth, participation in sports or entertainment, a political position, or a connection to another celebrity. Unlike *famous* or *notable*, the term usually implies a favorable public image. Historian Greg Jenner argues that the earliest celebrities lived in the early 1700s. In [[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greece]], athletes were welcomed home as heroes, and [[Julius Caesar]] appeared on a coin in his lifetime. [[Lord Byron]] became a celebrity in 1812 after publishing the first two cantos of *Childe Harold's Pilgrimage*. Juliet John has called [[Charles Dickens]] the first self-made global media star of the age of mass culture. In 1895, [[Oscar Wilde]] became the subject of "one of the first celebrity trials."

Cultivated plant of the species *Apium graveolens*. Celery belongs to the [[Apiaceae|Apiaceae]] family and has been used as a vegetable since ancient times. Selective breeding has produced stalk celery, leaf celery and celeriac, which is cultivated for its large edible hypocotyl. Celery is eaten raw in [[Salad|salads]], cooked in soups and stews, or juiced, and its seeds are used as a spice. It was cultivated in [[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greece]], and [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptians]] placed it in funeral garlands. In England it was once regarded as a cleansing [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]] against [[Scurvy|scurvy]], and its season was extended to run from September to April by the 19th century. [[Carl Linnaeus]] described the species in 1753.

Branch of astronomy concerned with the motions and gravitational interactions of objects in space. It applies [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]] to stars and planets to produce ephemeris data, often using a [[Coordinate system|coordinate system]] centered on the Sun. Newtonian mechanics predicts the future positions of two gravitationally bound bodies and confirms [[Kepler's laws of planetary motion|Kepler's laws]]; general relativity must be included when one body is very massive. Three-body problems cannot be solved exactly, so perturbation theory gives approximations. [[Isaac Newton]]'s *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* (1687) provided the foundation, and [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] introduced the name over a century later. In 1762, [[Leonhard Euler]] found three equilibrium points along a line through two primary masses; in 1772 [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] found two more, now called [[Lagrange point|Lagrange points]].

Position fixing by sighting stars, the [[Sun|Sun]] and other bodies. The practice relies on timed angular measurements, or sights, between a body and the visible [[Horizon|horizon]], and it does not depend on dead reckoning or electronic positioning. Two sights give two lines of position that intersect at the observer's location. The simplest method, noon sight navigation, uses one observation of the Sun's altitude at local noon, combined with the time at the [[Prime meridian|prime meridian]], to give a [[Latitude|latitude]] and [[Longitude|longitude]] fix. The [[Moon]], a planet, [[Polaris]] or one of 57 other navigational stars can be used in the same way. The method was used in the Apollo space program and remains in use on many satellites. Despite the dominance of [[Satellite navigation|satellite navigation]], it remains a backup for maritime and aviation safety.

Conceptual tool in astronomy and navigation. It is an abstract sphere of arbitrarily large radius, concentric with [[Earth|Earth]], onto which objects in the sky are conceived as projected regardless of their distance. The [[Equator|celestial equator]] divides it into northern and southern hemispheres. Because it is so large, parallel lines appear to meet at a single point on it, much as in graphical [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]]. Nearby objects such as the [[Moon]] show [[Parallax|parallax]], a small offset from a mean position that observers can calculate. Astronomers use the sphere for coordinates analogous to [[Latitude|latitude]] and [[Longitude|longitude]], so that a position such as the Moon's can be given in equatorial coordinates.

Cuban-American singer known as the Queen of Salsa. She rose to fame in Cuba during the 1950s singing guarachas and other Afro-Cuban styles, and she was a vocalist for the group Sonora Matancera from 1950 to 1965. After the [[Cuban Revolution|Cuban Revolution]] nationalized the music industry in 1960, she left Cuba, first living in [[Mexico|Mexico]] and then settling in the [[United States|United States]]. She became a symbol of the Cuban exile community. In the 1970s she joined Fania Records and became strongly associated with [[Salsa music|salsa]]. She sold over 30 million records and won two [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]] and three Latin Grammy Awards. Her catchphrase, "¡Azúcar!" ("Sugar!"), became a symbol of salsa. She was posthumously inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

State of voluntarily being unmarried and sexually abstinent. The term is often associated with religious officials or devotees. In its narrow sense it applies only to those unmarried by a sacred vow or religious conviction, and more broadly it means abstinence from sexual activity. The Hindu concept of brahmacharya encourages celibacy in youth and later as a path to spiritual liberation. [[Jainism|Jainism]] required complete celibacy even for young monks, and [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] is similar. In [[Christianity|Christianity]], Catholic priests, monks and nuns have normally taken vows of celibacy for centuries. [[Judaism|Judaism]] and [[Islam|Islam]] have denounced celibacy, though the Essenes practiced it, and one [[Hadith|hadith]] reports that [[Muhammad|Muhammad]] rejected it. Celibacy is considered distinct from [[Asexuality|asexuality]].

Canadian singer, entrepreneur and philanthropist. Dubbed the "Queen of Power Ballads", she has sold over 200 million records worldwide, making her one of the best-selling musical artists of all time. She won the Eurovision Song Contest 1988 representing Switzerland. The theme "My Heart Will Go On" for *Titanic* (1997) became one of the best-selling singles. She has won five [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]] and is one of the highest-grossing touring artists.

Study of the structure, function and behavior of the basic units of life. Cell biology, or cytology, encompasses both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, with subtopics including metabolism, cell communication, the [[Cell cycle|cell cycle]] and biochemistry. Research uses microscopy, cell culture and cell fractionation, and it is essential to biomedical research into [[Cancer|cancer]] and other diseases. The field is interconnected with [[Genetics|genetics]], [[Molecular biology|molecular biology]], [[Microbiology|microbiology]] and [[Immunology|immunology]]. [[Robert Hooke]] described cells in 1665, and in 1838 Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann formulated the cell theory. [[Rudolf Virchow]] later added that all cells come from the division of pre-existing cells. Viruses are not considered in cell biology, because they lack the characteristics of living cells.

Events leading to the division of a cell into two daughter cells. In eukaryotes, including animal, plant and [[Protist|protist]] cells, the cycle consists of interphase and the M phase, which includes [[Mitosis|mitosis]] and cytokinesis. During interphase the cell grows and replicates its [[DNA replication|DNA]], and checkpoints control whether it proceeds. Cells that stop dividing enter a resting G0 phase; many [[Neuron|neurons]] remain there indefinitely. In [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]] such as bacteria and archaea, DNA replication occurs during the C period. Repeated cycles let a multicellular organism develop from a fertilized egg and regenerate tissues such as [[Skin|skin]]. Dysregulation of the controls, often through [[Mutation|mutations]], can lead to uncontrolled proliferation, a hallmark of [[Cancer|cancer]].

Semipermeable lipid bilayer that separates a cell's interior from its surroundings. It is usually made of phospholipids and glycolipids. [[Eukaryote|Eukaryotes]] and some [[Archaea|archaea]] also contain sterols such as [[Cholesterol|cholesterol]], which maintain fluidity at different temperatures. Membrane proteins act as transporters and enzymes. The membrane is selectively permeable to [[Ion|ions]] and organic molecules, and it is involved in [[Cell signaling|cell signaling]] and adhesion. It is also the attachment surface for the [[Cytoskeleton|cytoskeleton]] inside the cell and for extracellular structures such as the [[Cell wall|cell wall]]. [[Robert Hooke]]'s discovery of cells in 1665 led to the cell theory. In 1925 Gorter and Grendel proposed a lipid bilayer, and in 1972 Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model.
